fact: Its ancestor is the African wildcat. Grain stores drew in rodents, and rodents drew in the cat.

name: Snail
fact: A shelled gastropod. Some freshwater species are, indirectly, among the deadliest animals to people.

name: Plasmodium
fact: A single-celled parasite genus that replicates inside red blood cells. Five species infect humans.

name: Toxoplasma gondii
fact: Cats are its only sexual host. Roughly half of people alive may carry it, mostly without symptoms.

name: Giardia
fact: A tough cyst form can stay infectious in cold water for up to three months, waiting to be swallowed.

name: Entamoeba histolytica
fact: An amoeba that mostly infects humans and other primates, and almost nothing else.

name: Trichomonas vaginalis
fact: A flagellated protozoan spread by direct sexual contact — no other route reliably passes it on.

name: Cryptosporidium
fact: Its oocyst shrugs off ordinary chlorine, which is why it's a real hazard even in treated water.

name: Ascaris lumbricoides
fact: Up to a billion people carry it. A single female can lay 200,000 eggs a day.

name: Hookworm
fact: Doesn't wait to be swallowed — its larvae simply burrow straight through bare skin.

name: Pinworm
fact: Its entire life cycle happens inside one human gut — humans are its only known host.

name: Trichinella spiralis
fact: The smallest nematode known to parasitize humans, yet one female can produce 1,500 larvae.

name: Wuchereria bancrofti
fact: Its larvae peak in the blood between 10 pm and 4 am, timed to when the night-biting mosquito feeds.

name: Taenia solium
fact: The pork tapeworm can grow past 8 metres long from a single scolex barely a millimetre wide.

name: Taenia saginata
fact: The beef tapeworm can top 22 metres and live in a human gut for 25 years.

name: Schistosoma
fact: A blood fluke that needs a freshwater snail as a stepping stone before it can reach a person at all.

name: Clonorchis sinensis
fact: The Chinese liver fluke can live 30 years in one host, passing through a snail and a fish to get there.

name: Head Louse
fact: Cannot jump or fly at all — it only spreads by direct head-to-head contact.

name: Body Louse
fact: Lives and lays its eggs in clothing seams, not on the body it feeds from.

name: Scabies Mite
fact: A burrowing female lays two or three eggs a day in a skin tunnel until her four-week life ends there.

name: Bed Bug
fact: Never lives on its host — it hides in dark seams nearby, like a mattress, between blood meals.

name: Malaria
fact: Fever comes in waves timed to red blood cells bursting open, all at once, every one to three days.

name: Toxoplasmosis
fact: Caught from cyst-laden undercooked meat as easily as from a cat's litter box.

name: Giardiasis
fact: Swallowing only a handful of cysts is enough to start an infection.

name: Amoebiasis
fact: Kills more than 55,000 people worldwide a year, mostly through amoebic dysentery.

name: Trichinosis
fact: First symptoms can appear in as little as twelve hours after eating the wrong meat.

name: Lymphatic Filariasis
fact: Adult worms block the body's own lymph vessels — the swelling of elephantiasis follows from there.

name: Schistosomiasis
fact: The second-most economically devastating parasitic disease on Earth, after malaria alone.

name: Gourd
fact: A Cucurbitaceae fruit that, dried out, leaves a hollow, hard shell — a container waiting to happen.

name: Mbira
fact: Zimbabwe's thumb piano: metal tines on a hardwood board, each tine a different length for a different pitch.

name: Gong
fact: A bronze disc quenched from red heat so it can be hammered soft, then hardened again by reheating.

name: Cymbal
fact: Cast bronze, lathed thin — cutting can shave off two-thirds the blank's weight, carving in the tone grooves.

name: Bell
fact: Cast from bell metal, a bronze around 23% tin — the ratio empirically settled on for the best tone.

name: Xylophone
fact: Wooden bars cut to length and struck — as with the marimba, longer bars ring lower, shorter bars higher.

name: Angklung
fact: West Javanese bamboo tubes tuned to a note, shaken so the tubes knock inside their own bamboo frame.

name: Maraca
fact: A dried gourd shell with a handful of pebbles or seeds sealed inside, shaken for the rattle.

name: Djembe
fact: A West African goblet drum carved from one log while the wood is still green, headed with goatskin.

name: Tabla
fact: The North Indian hand drum pair's black tuning spot, the syahi, is iron filings bound in a starch paste.

name: Timpani
fact: A copper kettle under a skin head — almost alone among drums, it can be tuned to a definite pitch.

name: Daf
fact: A Middle Eastern and Central Asian frame drum ringed inside with dozens of small jingling metal rings.

name: Guitar
fact: A hollow wood body resonates strings plucked or strummed by hand, no bow and no hammer involved.

name: Violin
fact: Its strings are bowed, not plucked — and the bow hair needs pine-resin rosin to actually grip and sound them.

name: Morin Khuur
fact: Mongolia's horsehead fiddle: strings and bow both traditionally horsehair, scroll carved as a horse's head.

name: Sitar
fact: A hollowed calabash gourd resonates metal strings — plus a set that vibrate on their own, never plucked.

name: Kora
fact: A West African 21-string harp-lute: a gourd sliced in half and sealed with cow skin as its resonator.

name: Piano
fact: A cast-iron frame holds up to 20 tons of string tension; felt-covered hammers strike the strings, not fingers.

name: Flute
fact: Holes cut along a tube shorten or lengthen the vibrating air column inside it, and that sets the pitch.

name: Pan Flute
fact: Many tubes of different lengths bound side by side, each one closed at the bottom and sounding one note.

name: Trumpet
fact: Brass tubing bent twice into a loop; the player's own buzzing lips against the mouthpiece make the sound.

name: Didgeridoo
fact: An Aboriginal Australian drone pipe — traditionally a eucalyptus branch termites hollowed out first.

name: Bagpipes
fact: An airtight animal-skin bag, squeezed by the arm, feeds reed pipes so the sound never stops for breath.

name: Shofar
fact: A ram's horn with no mouthpiece at all — heat softens its keratin enough to flatten and straighten it.

name: Theremin
fact: Played without ever being touched: a hand's distance from an antenna changes the circuit's own pitch.

name: Electric Guitar
fact: A vibrating steel string disturbs a magnet's field and induces current in a coil — no hollow body needed.

name: Synthesizer
fact: Generates its waveform electronically from scratch, rather than amplifying a vibration that already exists.

name: Producer
fact: Makes its own food from sunlight instead of eating anything — the base of every food chain.

name: Primary Consumer
fact: Eats producers directly and nothing else — the first animal step in a food chain, a herbivore.

name: Secondary Consumer
fact: A carnivore eating the herbivores that ate the plants — one rung above a primary consumer.

name: Decomposer
fact: Fungi and bacteria that feed on waste and the dead, turning it back into nutrients plants can use.

name: Trophic Level
fact: An organism's rung on the food chain — producer, then herbivore, then the carnivores above it.

name: Food Chain
fact: A straight line of who-eats-whom, from a producer up through consumers to whatever eats last.

name: Food Web
fact: Every real ecosystem's food chains tangled together — the actual network, not one single line.

name: Apex Predator
fact: Sits at the top of a food chain with few or no natural predators of its own left to eat it.

name: Trophic Cascade
fact: Remove a top predator and the effects ripple down every level below it — rarely simply, or fully.

name: Sea Urchin
fact: Grazes algae and kelp holdfasts with its teeth; enough of them can strip a seafloor bare.

name: Sea Otter
fact: Bites through a sea urchin's spines from underneath and licks out the soft contents inside.

name: Kelp Forest
fact: Dense underwater kelp, kept alive by otters eating the urchins that would otherwise graze it bare.

name: Keystone Species
fact: A species whose effect on its ecosystem is far bigger than its numbers alone would suggest.

name: Mutualism
fact: Two species, each genuinely better off for the other's presence — not one exploiting the other.

name: Commensalism
fact: One species benefits from the other, which is left neither better nor worse off by it.

name: Parasitism
fact: One organism lives on or in another and feeds off it, causing the host real, one-sided harm.

name: Whale Barnacle
fact: Embeds in whale skin and filters passing plankton with feathery limbs, usually at no cost to the whale.

name: Pioneer Species
fact: The first life to colonise bare ground — often lichen or moss — before anything else can take hold.

name: Ecological Succession
fact: How a community of species changes over time, one wave of colonisers replaced by the next.

name: Climax Community
fact: The stable, self-sustaining end stage of succession — the community that stops replacing itself.

name: Tundra
fact: Permafrost keeps the subsoil frozen year-round, so nothing taller than moss and lichen can root.

name: Desert
fact: Under 250 mm of rain a year defines it; little there stores water like a cactus's swollen stem.

name: Taiga
fact: The world's largest land biome — a belt of pine, spruce and larch across the subarctic.

name: Tropical Rainforest
fact: At least 1.68 m of rain a year, and a canopy so dense the forest floor gets 2% of the sunlight.

name: Limiting Factor
fact: Growth is capped by whichever resource is scarcest, not by the total of everything available.

name: Carrying Capacity
fact: The largest population an environment's food, water and space can sustain before growth stops.

name: Mountain
fact: Continental crust that collided and had nowhere to go but up — the Himalayas are still rising.

name: Ocean Trench
fact: The seafloor sagging where one plate bends and dives beneath another. The Mariana reaches 10,994 m.

name: Volcano
fact: A vent to a magma chamber. Alternating layers of lava and ash, erupted again and again, build the cone.

name: Rift Valley
fact: A continent stretched thin enough to crack: the block between two faults drops as the land splits.

name: Floodplain
fact: Flat land beside a river, built up flood by flood from the thin layer of silt each overflow leaves.

name: Meander
fact: Fast water wears the outer bank away, slow water drops sand on the inner one, and the bend migrates sideways.

name: Oxbow Lake
fact: A meander looped back on itself until its own neck was cut through, stranding the old bend as a lake.

name: River Delta
fact: A river hits still water, slows, and can no longer carry its load — the sediment drops and builds land.

name: Canyon
fact: A river cutting down through rock lifted thousands of feet beneath it — the Grand Canyon's whole story.

name: Waterfall
fact: Hard rock over soft: the soft layer erodes faster, and the drop between them grows a little every year.

name: Sea Cliff
fact: Waves cut a notch at the rock's foot; the overhang above eventually has nothing left to stand on.

name: Sea Cave
fact: Waves force their way into a crack in the cliff and hollow it out — always along an existing weakness.

name: Sea Arch
fact: A sea cave that finally breaks all the way through a thin headland, leaving an opening beneath the rock.

name: Sea Stack
fact: An arch's roof gives way at last, and what is left standing apart from the cliff is the stack.

name: Estuary
fact: Where a river's fresh water meets the moon-pulled tide and the two measurably mix, rather than staying apart.

name: Lagoon
fact: Shallow water fenced off from the open sea by a narrow bar of sand, with only a thin inlet through.

name: Glacier
fact: Snow that piled up faster than it melted, for centuries, compressed to ice, and is now sliding downhill.

name: Moraine
fact: A glacier works like a conveyor belt: it carries stone for miles and drops it all at the melting end.

name: Iceberg
fact: A slab of a glacier that calved — broke free — and now drifts on the salt water it did not come from.

name: Fjord
fact: A glacier gouges a valley far below sea level; the ice retreats, and the sea moves in to fill it.

name: Cavern
fact: Rainwater turned faintly acidic by carbon dioxide dissolves limestone along a crack for centuries.

name: Sinkhole
fact: A cavern hollowed out below keeps growing until the ground above it can no longer hold its own weight.

name: Plateau
fact: High ground, flat on top: a broad slab of crust swollen upward by magma rising underneath it.

name: Mesa
fact: A plateau's edge eaten back by weather until an isolated, flat-topped island of hard caprock remains.

name: Butte
fact: A mesa worn narrower still, until almost nothing is left of the caprock that was protecting it.

name: Caldera
fact: A magma chamber empties in a great eruption, and the volcano above it has nothing left to hold it up.

name: Geyser
fact: Groundwater heated past boiling but held down by its own weight, until it flashes to steam all at once.

name: Eagle
fact: Hunts open country from cliffside nests, diving at up to 320 km/h to take prey.

name: Jaguar
fact: The only big cat that regularly cracks turtle shells, killing with a bite to the skull.

name: Turquoise
fact: A hydrous phosphate of copper and aluminium -- one of the oldest gemstones ever mined.

name: Quetzalcoatl
fact: Aztec feathered-serpent god of wind, Venus and learning. The name means Precious Serpent.

name: Tezcatlipoca
fact: Aztec god of night and sorcery. His name means Smoking Mirror, for the obsidian he is shown in.

name: Huitzilopochtli
fact: Aztec sun and war god, patron of Tenochtitlan, born fully armed from Coatlicue.

name: Tlaloc
fact: Aztec rain god known by his goggle eyes and fangs; ruled the paradise of Tlalocan.

name: Coatlicue
fact: Aztec earth goddess, 'Serpent Skirt' -- mother of Huitzilopochtli and of the stars.

name: Tonatiuh
fact: Aztec sun god of the current, fifth cosmic age; demanded sacrifice to keep moving.

name: Mictlantecuhtli
fact: Skeletal Aztec god of the dead, king of Mictlan's lowest level.

name: Xiuhtecuhtli
fact: Aztec fire god, the Turquoise Lord -- turquoise was fire's own stone to him.

name: Centeotl
fact: Aztec young maize god, his face marked by a black line from brow to jaw.

name: Xolotl
fact: Dog-headed Aztec god who guides the dead through Mictlan; the axolotl bears his name.

name: Fifth Sun
fact: The current Aztec cosmic age, born when two gods leapt into a divine bonfire.

name: Sun Stone
fact: A 24-tonne Aztec basalt disc carved under Moctezuma II, recording the cosmic ages.

name: Mictlan
fact: Aztec underworld of nine levels; the dead take four years to reach the deepest one.

name: Kukulkan
fact: Yucatec Maya feathered serpent; his shadow descends Chichen Itza's pyramid each equinox.

name: Itzamna
fact: Maya creator god credited with inventing writing; often shown as an aged sky lord.

name: Ixchel
fact: Aged Maya jaguar goddess of medicine, childbirth and water; consort of Itzamna.

name: Chaac
fact: Maya rain god, long-nosed, who strikes clouds with a lightning axe to bring rain.

name: Ek Chuah
fact: Maya god of merchants, travellers and cacao, honoured each year in its harvest season.

name: Popol Vuh
fact: K'iche' Maya sacred text: creation, the Hero Twins, and a people's own history.

name: Hero Twins
fact: Hunahpu and Xbalanque, the Maya Hero Twins who out-tricked the lords of Xibalba.

name: Xibalba
fact: The K'iche' Maya underworld, 'place of fright,' ruled by One Death and Seven Death.

name: Cacao of the Gods
fact: Cacao's mythic origin as a gift from the gods -- hence its genus name, 'food of the gods.'

name: Open-Pit Mining
fact: Dug in stepped benches, with haul roads spiralling up the walls — a million tons a day from the biggest pits.

name: Strip Mining
fact: Digs a shallow seam one long trench at a time, burying each strip's waste in the void left by the last.

name: Mountaintop Removal
fact: Blasts up to 120 metres off a summit to reach thin coal, dumping the rock in the next valley over.

name: Placer Mining
fact: Washes loose sand and gravel through water and lets density sort out anything worth keeping.

name: Room-and-Pillar Mining
fact: Digs rooms out of a seam while leaving pillars of untouched rock standing to hold the roof up.

name: Longwall Mining
fact: A shearer cuts a long coal face while supports advance and the roof is let collapse behind them.

name: Block Caving
fact: Undercuts a huge ore column and lets gravity fracture it, falling into tunnels dug below.

name: Bauxite
fact: Aluminium's ore, and it sits so close to the surface there's barely any overburden to remove.

name: Spodumene
fact: A lithium aluminium silicate that crystallises in granite pegmatite — most hard-rock lithium's source.

name: Bastnäsite
fact: A rare-earth fluorocarbonate — almost all of Mountain Pass, California's rare earths ride in this one mineral.

name: Leopard
fact: Leopards drag kills heavier than themselves into trees — once a giraffe calf hauled 5.7 m up.

name: Snow Leopard
fact: Its tail is thick with stored fat and fur, worn like a blanket over its face while it sleeps.

name: Cheetah
fact: Goes 0 to 97 km/h in under 3 seconds — faster off the line than most sports cars.

name: Cougar
fact: Ranges from the Yukon to the southern Andes — the widest span of any wild land mammal.

name: Red Fox
fact: Earthworms can supply over 60% of its calories some months — hunted mostly by ear.

name: Coyote
fact: Hunts in loose bands to bring down prey too big for one alone, a habit noted since 1805.

name: African Wild Dog
fact: Some Serengeti packs specialise in hunting adult zebra six times their own weight.

name: Polar Bear
fact: Waits motionless for hours by a seal's breathing hole in the ice, then strikes the instant it surfaces.

name: Giant Panda
fact: Evolved an extra 'thumb' from a wrist bone just to grip bamboo, despite being classed a carnivore.

name: Sun Bear
fact: The smallest bear has the longest tongue of any bear, for licking honey from tight spaces.

name: Gorilla
fact: Western lowland gorillas eat far more fruit than mountain gorillas, who barely touch it.

name: Chimpanzee
fact: Chimps strip leaves off twigs to fish termites from mounds, the first wild tool use ever recorded.

name: Orangutan
fact: The most arboreal great ape — it crosses the canopy climbing and swinging, rarely touching ground.

name: Olive Baboon
fact: Troops hunt cooperatively on the open savanna, taking prey as large as young gazelles.

name: Ring-tailed Lemur
fact: Sunbathes every cold morning, sitting upright and facing the sun like a devotee.

name: Bald Eagle
fact: Builds the largest tree nest of any North American bird — one weighed over a metric ton.

name: Peregrine Falcon
fact: The fastest animal on Earth — it can exceed 320 km/h in its hunting dive.

name: Snowy Owl
fact: Unlike most owls, it hunts mainly by daylight across the open Arctic tundra.

name: Turkey Vulture
fact: Locates carrion by smell, an ability most birds lack, sniffing out decay from the air.

name: King Cobra
fact: Its genus name means 'snake-eater' — king cobras prey chiefly on other snakes.

name: Komodo Dragon
fact: The world's largest lizard, up to 3 m and 150 kg, with a genuinely venomous bite.

name: Gila Monster
fact: The only venomous lizard native to the US — it chews its venom in through grooved teeth.

name: Nile Crocodile
fact: Its bite force measures about 22 kN — among the strongest of any living animal.

name: American Alligator
fact: The female guards her mud nest for 65 days, then carries hatchlings to water in her mouth.

name: Golden Poison Frog
fact: The most toxic vertebrate known by weight — one wild frog carries enough poison for 10-20 people.

name: American Bullfrog
fact: A voracious ambush predator whose stomach contents have included snakes, birds and bats.

name: Cane Toad
fact: Introduced to Australia in 1935 to fight cane beetles that lived too high on the stalks to reach.

name: Axolotl
fact: Unlike other salamanders, it never leaves the water or metamorphoses — it keeps its gills for life.

name: Fire Salamander
fact: Its black-and-yellow pattern is a warning label for the neurotoxin it secretes from its skin.

name: Stem
fact: The plant's upright main axis — bears leaves and buds, and pipes water and food between root and leaf.

name: Node
fact: The point on a stem where a leaf attaches; buds and branches start here too.

name: Internode
fact: The stretch of stem between two nodes — it elongates to space the leaves out.

name: Terminal Bud
fact: The bud at a stem's growing tip; its auxin keeps the buds below it suppressed.

name: Axillary Bud
fact: A dormant side-bud sitting in a leaf's axil, ready to become a new branch.

name: Leaf Scar
fact: The corky mark a fallen leaf leaves behind, right where it once attached.

name: Lenticel
fact: A loosely packed pore in bark that lets a woody stem's living tissue breathe.

name: Root Cap
fact: The tough cap of cells shielding a root's tip as it pushes through soil.

name: Root Meristem
fact: A knot of ceaselessly dividing cells behind the root cap — source of every new root cell.

name: Elongation Zone
fact: Where new root cells stop dividing and stretch lengthwise, pushing the tip forward.

name: Root Hair
fact: A fine tubular outgrowth that multiplies a root's surface for soaking up water.

name: Cotyledon
fact: An embryonic seed-leaf, often the first green tissue to unfurl as a seed sprouts.

name: Monocot
fact: A flowering plant that sprouts with one cotyledon — grasses, lilies, palms, orchids.

name: Dicot
fact: A flowering plant that sprouts with two cotyledons — historically over half of species.

name: Kapok
fact: Ceiba pentandra, the 'cotton tree' — a rainforest giant with huge plank buttress roots.

name: Buttress Root
fact: Wide, thin plank roots that stop a tall, shallow-rooted rainforest tree toppling over.

name: Brace Root
fact: Adventitious roots from maize's above-ground stem nodes, arching down to prop it up.

name: Ivy
fact: Hedera helix: an evergreen climber that grips trees and walls with clinging roots.

name: Clinging Root
fact: A root that glues itself to a surface for grip, instead of drinking from the soil.

name: Aerial Root
fact: A green, chlorophyll-bearing root some orchids hang in open air — no soil needed.

name: Pneumatophore
fact: A mangrove's snorkel root, poking up out of waterlogged mud to pull in air.

name: Movable Type
fact: Cast from lead, tin and antimony in a hand mould — one reusable piece per letter.

name: Printing Press
fact: A screw-driven bar presses inked type onto paper. Gutenberg, working from about 1436.

name: Telescope
fact: A convex lens focuses light, a concave eyepiece spreads it out magnified. Galileo, 1609.

name: Steam Engine
fact: Watt split the condenser from the cylinder in 1769, so the cylinder never cools between strokes.

name: Barometer
fact: Mercury in a sealed glass tube, held up by the weight of the air alone. Torricelli, 1643.

name: Pendulum Clock
fact: A pendulum's swing takes the same time regardless of its width, so it can pace a clock. Huygens, 1656.

name: Cotton Gin
fact: Iron teeth comb cotton through slots too narrow for the seeds. Whitney, 1793.

name: Sewing Machine
fact: An eye-pointed needle carries thread through cloth to meet a shuttle's thread below. Howe, 1845.

name: Elevator
fact: A spring drives pawls into the guide rails' teeth the instant the hoisting rope goes slack. Otis, 1852.

name: Telegraph
fact: A key switches current down a wire; the current switches an electromagnet at the far end. Morse, 1844.

name: Telephone
fact: An iron diaphragm near a magnet turns sound into a matching current, and back again. Bell, 1876.

name: Radio
fact: A discharging capacitor oscillates across a spark gap and radiates from a wire antenna. Marconi, 1896.

name: Vacuum Tube
fact: A heated filament boils electrons into a vacuum; they cross to the plate only one way. Fleming, 1904.

name: Phonograph
fact: A vibrating needle indents hill-and-dale grooves into tinfoil on a turning cylinder. Edison, 1877.

name: X-Ray
fact: Electrons striking the wall of an evacuated tube throw off radiation that photographs bone. Röntgen, 1895.

name: Camera Obscura
fact: Light through a small hole lands inverted and reversed on the far wall of a dark box.

name: Photographic Plate
fact: Silver fumed with iodine forms silver iodide, a compound so light-sensitive that exposure darkens it.

name: Photograph
fact: A camera projects onto a light-sensitive plate; mercury vapor develops the invisible result. Daguerre, 1839.

name: Ether
fact: Sulfuric acid dehydrates ethanol into ether — the anesthetic Morton demonstrated in 1846.

name: Integrated Circuit
fact: Every part of a circuit, not just the transistors, built into one block of semiconductor. Kilby, 1958.

name: Microprocessor
fact: An entire CPU's arithmetic, logic and control on a single chip. Intel's 4004, 1971.

name: Internal Combustion Engine
fact: Otto compressed the fuel-air mixture in a cylinder before igniting it, for far higher efficiency. 1876.

name: Airplane
fact: A cambered wing lifts, warped wingtips steer, a chain-driven propeller pulls. Kitty Hawk, 1903.

name: Typewriter
fact: A struck key swings a metal bar that prints its letter, reversed on the bar, through an inked ribbon.

name: Herrerasaurus
fact: A basal saurischian near the theropod/sauropodomorph split; a bitten skull shows it fought its own kind.

name: Dilophosaurus
fact: Early Jurassic theropod with air-filled, bird-like bones and a pair of thin display crests, not weapons.

name: Ceratosaurus
fact: A blade-toothed predator named for the display horn on its snout, likely too fragile for real combat.

name: Carnotaurus
fact: Paired brow horns and arms so tiny its fingers fused — the first theropod found with real skin impressions.

name: Giganotosaurus
fact: A carcharodontosaurid rivaling Tyrannosaurus in size, with jaws built to slice prey, not crush its bones.

name: Baryonyx
fact: Its huge thumb claw and crocodile-like snout matched a stomach holding fish scales and a young iguanodontid.

name: Therizinosaurus
fact: A herbivorous theropod with the longest claws of any known animal, hooked to pull branches within reach.

name: Oviraptor
fact: Named 'egg thief' for a skull found near a nest; later finds proved it died brooding its own eggs.

name: Gallimimus
fact: An ostrich-mimic that could run 42-56 km/h, with a toothless beak suited to plants and small prey alike.

name: Microraptor
fact: A crow-sized, four-winged dromaeosaur that glided between trees, its gut once holding fish, bird, and mammal.

name: Diplodocus
fact: A long, low-browsing sauropod whose whip-thin tail held about 80 vertebrae and roughly half its body length.

name: Massospondylus
fact: A basal, bipedal sauropodomorph whose nesting ground is the oldest known evidence of nest-site fidelity.

name: Euoplocephalus
fact: An armored ankylosaurid with bony plates even over its eyelids and a tail club that could fracture bone.

name: Psittacosaurus
fact: A parrot-beaked early ceratopsian, some found with quill-like bristles down the tail and gastroliths inside.

name: Styracosaurus
fact: A centrosaurine with a long nose horn and a frill ringed by spikes, likely for display more than defense.

name: Pentaceratops
fact: Its name means 'five-horned face' — a nose horn, two long brow horns, and two frill-edge cheek points.

name: Camptosaurus
fact: A basal iguanodontian whose heavily worn teeth show a lifetime of chewing tough, fibrous vegetation.

name: Maiasaura
fact: Its name means 'good mother lizard' — hatchlings with unworn legs but worn teeth show adults fed the nest.

name: Drilling Rig
fact: Bores rows of blast-holes up to 27cm across and 40+ metres deep before a bench is ever blasted.

name: Dragline Excavator
fact: Strip mining's biggest machine, almost always run on grid power through a trailing cable, not diesel.

name: Diesel-Electric Drive
fact: Skips the gearbox: a generator makes electricity, and motors turn it back into torque at the wheel.

name: Haul Truck
fact: The largest, BelAZ's 75710, carries 450 tonnes on eight tyres 4 metres across.

name: Continuous Miner
fact: A rotating drum rips coal straight off the face, replacing separate cutting, drilling and blasting crews.

name: Longwall Shearer
fact: The machine longwall mining is named for: twin drums shear coal off the face as supports advance behind it.

name: Locomotive
fact: Diesel-electric transmission reached railways before mining trucks — most freight locomotives use it.

name: Crusher
fact: A gyratory or jaw crusher, essentially a moving steel jaw, breaks boulder-sized ore to fist-sized chunks.

name: Ball Mill
fact: A rotating steel drum tumbling with forged steel balls grinds crushed ore down to sand-sized grains.

name: Flotation Cell
fact: Blows air through a ground-ore slurry so valuable, chemically-treated grains stick to bubbles and float off.

name: Tailings
fact: The roughly 99% of ground rock flotation doesn't want, pumped as slurry to a storage dam.

name: Conveyor Belt
fact: A closed loop of reinforced rubber slung between pulleys — cheaper per tonne-kilometre than trucking.

name: Stockpile
fact: Buffers a mine's day-to-day grade swings by blending many truckloads of ore into one consistent pile.

name: Ore Railway
fact: A dedicated unit train, one commodity and one route — the record run was 7.35km long, 99,734 tonnes.

name: Bulk Terminal
fact: Where ore stops being a stockpile and becomes an export — Port Hedland alone ships 500+ million tonnes a year.

name: Bulk Carrier
fact: Capesize ships too big for the Suez or Panama Canal carry about 75% of the world's seaborne iron ore.

name: Piston
fact: Grey cast iron pistons and rings carry their own lubricant: graphite already inside the metal.

name: Axle
fact: A wheelset: two wheels fixed rigidly to one steel shaft, so they always turn together.

name: Bogie
fact: A pivoted frame under a rail car holding two or more axles, so a long car can still take a curve.

name: Steam locomotive
fact: Steam pushes a piston; a connecting rod turns that push into a crank pin on the driving wheel.

name: Diesel-electric locomotive
fact: The diesel engine never touches the wheels — it spins a generator that feeds traction motors.

name: Electric locomotive
fact: No engine on board — current from an overhead wire or third rail drives the motors directly.

name: Freight wagon
fact: An unpowered steel-framed car riding on bogies, built to be coupled into a train of many.

name: Hopper car
fact: A sloped floor and bottom gates dump bulk coal, ore or grain without anyone shovelling.

name: Tank car
fact: A cylindrical steel vessel for liquid or gas — some are lined in glass to protect the shell.

name: Flatcar
fact: No sides, no roof — an open deck for loads too big or heavy for any other kind of wagon.

name: Boxcar
fact: A fully enclosed wagon with sliding doors, built to keep general freight dry.

name: Caboose
fact: The crew's car at the back — a cupola let them watch the whole train roll by for trouble.

name: Coupler
fact: Push two cars together and the knuckle locks itself shut — no one stands between them.

name: Roller bearing
fact: Hardened chromium-steel rollers between two rings — the axle turns on them, not against them.

name: Plain bearing
fact: No rolling parts at all — the axle just slides in a graphite-lubricated sleeve.

name: Air brake
fact: Compressed air presses the shoe to the wheel — and clamps shut if the line ever breaks.

name: Block signal
fact: One train per block, always — a rail circuit senses the train itself, not a fixed timer.

name: Rail
fact: Hot-rolled steel, I-beam in cross-section — standard gauge sets the rails 1,435 mm apart.

name: Sleeper
fact: The crosstie that holds the gauge — wood needs creosote against rot; concrete needs none.

name: Ballast
fact: Sharp, angular crushed rock — the interlocking edges keep the sleepers from creeping.

name: Points
fact: A pair of tapered rails that pivot to send a train onto one track or another.

name: Rail yard
fact: Not a station — a ladder of switches sorts wagons onto tracks to build new trains.

name: Capacitor
fact: Two conductors and an insulating gap. Glass, ceramic, paper, even air can serve as that gap.

name: Accelerometer
fact: A silicon mass on springs. Acceleration shifts it, and a capacitor reads the shift as motion.

name: Photodiode
fact: Silicon answers light from 190 to 1100 nanometres — deep into the infrared a remote control uses.

name: Click Wheel
fact: A ring of electrodes under plastic. A fingertip's own capacitance tells it where the finger sits.

name: Flash Memory
fact: A gate buried in oxide traps electrons there for years — a bit that survives the power going off.

name: iPod
fact: Apple, 2001. A hard drive of songs, then flash memory, controlled by a touch-sensitive wheel.

name: Nike+iPod Sensor
fact: A pad under the insole radios a packet to the iPod once a second, running or not, for ten more.

name: Midsole Foam
fact: Foam rubber or EVA, both blown into closed gas cells — the give under a running shoe's arch.

name: Athletic Shoe
fact: A foam midsole over a rubber outsole, tuned to how much the wearer's foot naturally rolls inward.

name: Polarizer
fact: Iodine chains stretched straight through plastic film absorb light vibrating one way, pass the rest.

name: Liquid Crystal
fact: Reinitzer heated cholesteryl benzoate in 1888 and it melted twice, through a cloudy phase between.

name: Thin-Film Transistor
fact: A transistor grown on glass instead of cut from a wafer — one per pixel, switching it alone.

name: Liquid Crystal Cell
fact: One transistor, one crystal, repeated millions of times — every pixel twisted open or shut alone.

name: LCD Screen
fact: White light through two crossed polarizers with a twistable crystal between decides each pixel.

name: IMAX 3-D Projection
fact: Two lenses, two polarizing filters at right angles — one image per eye, sorted out by the glasses.

name: Laser Diode
fact: A diode's own cleaved faces work as mirrors, turning ordinary light emission into a coherent beam.

name: DVD Player
fact: A laser reads a spiral of pits by interference; Blu-ray's bluer laser reads pits four times smaller.

name: Photosite
fact: A capacitor built in silicon. Light frees electrons and the capacitor holds them, pixel by pixel.

name: CCD Sensor
fact: Boyle and Smith, 1969. Each photosite's charge shuffles down the row like a bucket brigade to be read.

name: Digital Camera
fact: A converter assigns each photosite's charge a binary number — light becomes a file, not a negative.

name: Magnetic Tape
fact: A magnetizable coating on a strip of plastic film — sound and picture stored as magnetism, not light.

name: VHS Cassette
fact: JVC's format beat Sony's sharper Betamax in the 1980s because its decks were cheaper and taped longer.

name: Magnetron
fact: A magnet spirals boiling-off electrons past cavities cut into a copper block, which ring at 2.45 GHz.

name: Microwave Oven
fact: Percy Spencer, 1946. A field flipping 2.45 billion times a second spins polar molecules, not just water.

name: Scanner
fact: Mirrors bounce light from the original onto a CCD array, one thin strip at a time as the head crawls.

name: Barcode Scanner
fact: A spinning mirror sweeps a laser across the bars up to 1,200 times a second; a detector reads the flicker.

name: Fingerprint Scanner
fact: A grid of capacitor plates under the surface — ridges sit closer than valleys, and that reads as a print.

name: Wii Remote
fact: A camera tracks two infrared LED clusters for pointing while an accelerometer senses the swing.

name: Superconducting Magnet
fact: Chilled below its critical temperature, its coil carries current with zero resistance.

name: MRI Scan
fact: Aligns hydrogen nuclei in the body's water and fat, then reads them relaxing back.

name: FDG
fact: Ordinary glucose with one hydroxyl swapped for radioactive fluorine-18.

name: Positron
fact: The electron's antimatter twin: identical mass, opposite charge.

name: PET Scan
fact: A detector ring times paired gamma rays, nanoseconds apart, to find where they began.

name: Transducer
fact: A piezoelectric crystal that turns an alternating voltage into a beam of sound.

name: Ultrasonic Wave
fact: A pressure wave in tissue, pitched far above the roughly 20,000 Hz a human ear can hear.

name: Echo
fact: Sound bounced back at a tissue boundary; its timing and strength reveal depth and density.

name: 4-D Ultrasound
fact: Thousands of 3-D slices a second, stitched into motion — time as the fourth dimension.

name: ICSI Needle
fact: A glass micropipette fine enough to carry one sperm straight through an egg's membrane.

name: Nerve
fact: A cable of axons carrying electrical impulses at up to 120 metres a second.

name: Myoelectric Signal
fact: An electrical twitch in a rerouted muscle, standing in for a hand that is no longer there.

name: Bionic Arm
fact: One rerouted nerve's old command still moves a prosthetic hand, via a skin sensor.

name: Robotic Surgery
fact: A surgeon's hand movements, scaled down and freed of tremor, move tiny remote instruments.

name: Hydraulic Pump
fact: A motor-driven pump that shuttles fluid between two chambers to push blood along.

name: Artificial Heart
fact: A titanium pump wired through the skin only by a magnetic field, never by a wire.

name: Reinforced Concrete
fact: Steel rebar gives concrete the tensile strength it lacks entirely on its own.

name: Curtain Wall
fact: A building's non-structural glass skin, carrying only its own weight, not the floors above.

name: Skyscraper
fact: A steel-and-concrete core takes the load; a hung glass skin merely keeps the weather out.

name: Laser
fact: Chromium ions in a flashed ruby rod drop back to the ground state in exact lockstep.

name: Holographic Plate
fact: Silver-halide emulsion on glass, fine-grained enough to record an interference pattern.

name: Hologram
fact: Not a picture: a recording of a light wave's phase, reconstructed by the same beam again.

name: Fullerene
fact: Sixty carbon atoms closed into a cage shaped exactly like a soccer ball.

name: Carbon Nanotube
fact: A single sheet of graphite's lattice, rolled into a seamless tube a few atoms wide.

name: STM Tip
fact: A tungsten wire etched electrochemically down to a point that ends in one atom.

name: Tunneling Microscope
fact: Electrons cross a vacuum gap they classically shouldn't, mapping a surface atom by atom.

name: Hadron Collider
fact: Superconducting magnets steer two proton beams to near light speed, then crash them together.

name: Wool Card
fact: A paddle set with fine wire teeth that combs locked wool fibres straight and parallel.

name: Carded Wool
fact: Every fibre now runs the same direction, and the trapped bits of straw and dirt are gone.

name: Felt
fact: No thread, no loom. Wet wool's own microscopic scales lock together under heat and rubbing.

name: Spindle
fact: A weighted rod that twists loose fibre into thread as it spins in the hand or against the thigh.

name: Spinning Wheel
fact: The wheel drives the spindle instead of a hand doing it — over ten times faster.

name: Loom
fact: A frame that holds the warp threads taut so the weft can be woven back and forth through them.

name: Flying Shuttle
fact: Kay's 1733 shuttle rode on wheels, so one weaver alone could work cloth twice as wide.

name: Knitting Needles
fact: Two tapered rods: one holds the loops, the other draws a fresh loop through each one.

name: Knitted Fabric
fact: One yarn meandering into interlocked loops — not two sets crossing at right angles like cloth.

name: Indigo
fact: A shrub in the bean family, field-grown across the tropics for the blue dye locked in its leaves.

name: Leuco-Indigo
fact: Indigo won't dissolve in water until fermentation turns it into this — pale yellow, not blue.

name: Madder
fact: A root grown over a metre long on purpose — the whole point is the red dye packed inside it.

name: Alizarin
fact: The exact anthraquinone molecule inside madder root that's actually responsible for the red.

name: Alum
fact: A double sulfate of aluminium — for centuries, the dye trade's single most common mordant.

name: Rose Madder
fact: Alizarin alone washes straight out. Bonded to alum, it becomes a dye that survives the wash.

name: Dyed Cloth
fact: Colour bonded into the fibre itself, not sitting on top of it — the difference a mordant makes.

name: Atomic Clock
fact: Quartz tuned to vibrate at the exact frequency of a caesium atom's transition.

name: Communications Satellite
fact: A radio transceiver with nothing to plug into, kept running by solar cells.

name: GPS Satellite
fact: 24 of these orbit twice daily, each one carrying an atomic clock.

name: GPS
fact: Times signals from four-plus satellites and trilaterates one point where they agree.

name: Cellular Telephone
fact: A telephone's mouthpiece and earpiece wired to a radio that hands off tower to tower.

name: Smartphone
fact: A cellular phone with a general-purpose microprocessor added — it computes now, not just calls.

name: Computer
fact: A microprocessor paired with memory for its program and data — the stored-program design.

name: Router
fact: Reads each packet's address and switches it out the right wire, one hop closer.

name: The Internet
fact: Not one network but many, glued by routers forwarding packets hop by hop.

name: Film Reel
fact: A cellulose strip coated with the same silver-bromide emulsion still photography uses.

name: Movie Camera
fact: A camera obscura whose lens exposes a moving film strip one frame at a time.

name: Film Projector
fact: A bright bulb shines through the same sprocketed film a camera exposed, onto a screen.

name: Cinematography
fact: A camera at 24 frames a second and a projector running them past a lamp at the same rate.

name: Television
fact: A radio tuned to a video channel instead of an audio one, feeding a screen.

name: Mutation
fact: A change in the DNA sequence, from a copying mistake or damage. You carry about 60 unique to you.

name: Natural Selection
fact: Mutations that help you survive or reproduce spread through a population; harmful ones tend to vanish.

name: Evolution
fact: Heritable change in a population's traits across generations — natural selection, given enough time.

name: Common Ancestor
fact: Every living thing on Earth traces back to one ancestral population, about four billion years ago.

name: Allele
fact: A different version of the same gene. You carry two of almost every one, one from each parent.

name: Genetic Diversity
fact: How many different alleles exist across a population's genes. Bigger pools survive change better.

name: Cystic Fibrosis
fact: A faulty chloride-channel gene clogs the lungs and gut with thick mucus. Inherited, not contagious.

name: Sickle Cell Anemia
fact: One swapped amino acid bends red blood cells into a sickle shape that jams in blood vessels.

name: Cancer
fact: Mutations disable the brakes on cell division, and a mass of runaway cells forms a tumor.

name: Gene Therapy
fact: Delivering a working copy of a gene into a patient's cells to make up for a faulty one.

name: CRISPR
fact: A bacterial defence system repurposed as molecular scissors that cut DNA at a chosen sequence.

name: Cloning
fact: Producing an individual with DNA identical to another's — plants and labs both know how.

name: Parthenogenesis
fact: An egg develops into an embryo without fertilization. The offspring is a clone of the mother.

name: De-extinction
fact: Splicing an extinct species' genes into a living relative's genome to bring back lost traits.

name: DNA Sequencing
fact: Reading out the exact order of bases in a stretch of DNA, one letter at a time.

name: Mitochondrial DNA
fact: DNA inside mitochondria, inherited only from the mother, unchanged down the maternal line.

name: DNA Profile
fact: A person's unique pattern of DNA markers, precise enough to match evidence to one person.

name: Wing spar
fact: The beam running the length of the wing that carries almost all of its bending load.

name: Wing
fact: A cambered airfoil at the right angle of attack turns air downward and gets pushed up in return.

name: Fuselage
fact: The main body. In a stressed-skin design the outer shell itself carries structural load.

name: Tailplane
fact: A small fixed aerofoil at the tail that balances the main wing's lift and holds the nose steady.

name: Aileron
fact: A hinged flap at the wingtip's trailing edge. One goes up as the other goes down, and the aircraft rolls.

name: Rudder
fact: A hinged panel on the fin at the tail, swinging the nose left or right — a ship's steering, borrowed.

name: Tail elevator
fact: A hinged panel on the tailplane's trailing edge. Deflect it and the nose pitches up or down.

name: Landing gear
fact: A wheel on an oleo strut, a telescoping tube of gas and oil that soaks up the shock of touchdown.

name: Propeller
fact: A spinning airfoil, twisted so every point along the blade meets the air at a useful angle.

name: Petroleum
fact: Buried marine algae and plankton, cooked by millions of years of heat and pressure into crude oil.

name: Jet fuel
fact: Kerosene: the fraction of crude oil that boils off between petrol and diesel.

name: Compressor
fact: Alternating spinning and fixed blades squeeze incoming air into a fraction of its intake volume.

name: Combustor
fact: Fuel burns continuously in a steady stream of compressed air, not stroke by stroke like a piston engine.

name: Turbine
fact: Blades in the hottest gas in the engine, spun by the exhaust and geared straight to the compressor.

name: Jet engine
fact: A turbine drives a compressor on the same shaft, with fuel burning continuously in between.

name: Turbofan
fact: A ducted fan bolted to the front of a jet engine; most of its thrust comes from air the core never touches.

name: Glider
fact: An aircraft with no engine at all, trading height for speed and finding air that rises faster than it sinks.

name: Hot air balloon
fact: Air heated by an open flame is less dense than the air around it, so the whole envelope floats.

name: Airship
fact: Unlike a balloon, it steers: engines and control surfaces added to a gas-filled envelope.

name: Rotor
fact: Long, narrow airfoils exactly like a wing's, spun around a hub so they make their own airspeed.

name: Helicopter
fact: A spinning rotor lifts it straight up with no runway, and a tail rotor stops the fuselage spinning too.

name: Parachute
fact: A wide canopy multiplies the drag of a falling body until it settles to a survivable speed.

name: Jet airliner
fact: A fuselage carried by engines that burn fuel continuously instead of turning a propeller.

name: Runway
fact: A paved strip long enough to reach flying speed on wheels, numbered for the compass heading it points.

name: Hangar
fact: A roof wide enough to clear a whole wingspan with no column standing in the way.

name: Taxiway
fact: Paved like a runway but marked yellow, not white — where aircraft move on their own engines, not full speed.

name: Control tower
fact: A glass-walled cab high enough to see the whole airfield, sequencing aircraft entirely by radio.

name: Airport
fact: Runways, taxiways, hangars and a tower, all working as one system to move aircraft, not just park them.

name: DNA Helicase
fact: A motor protein that burns ATP to unwind the double helix at a replication fork.

name: Primase
fact: Lays a short RNA primer on bare DNA — polymerase can only extend an end, never start one.

name: DNA Polymerase
fact: Adds nucleotides to a primer's 3' end, one at a time, reading the template strand.

name: Okazaki Fragment
fact: A short burst of DNA made on the lagging strand, later stitched together with the rest.

name: DNA Ligase
fact: Seals the nicks between Okazaki fragments into one unbroken strand.

name: DNA Replication
fact: Semiconservative copying: every new double helix keeps one old strand and one new one.

name: RNA Polymerase
fact: Binds a promoter, pries the helix open, and builds RNA against the exposed template.

name: Transcription
fact: DNA's sequence copied into RNA — the first of the two steps that build a protein.

name: Codon
fact: Three mRNA bases in a row. 64 combinations, 61 of them each naming one amino acid.

name: Anticodon
fact: The three bases on a tRNA that pair with a codon, matching amino acid to instruction.

name: Translation
fact: The ribosome reads codons three at a time and strings amino acids into a protein.

name: Intron
fact: Non-coding filler transcribed into pre-mRNA, then cut out before the message ships.

name: Exon
fact: The coding pieces of a transcript left over once splicing removes the introns.

name: Splicing
fact: The spliceosome cuts introns out and stitches exons together into mature mRNA.

name: Point Mutation
fact: One base pair swapped for another — silent, missense, or nonsense depending on where.

name: Frameshift Mutation
fact: Insert or delete bases not in threes and every codon downstream reads wrong.

name: Geological Mapping
fact: Rock types and structures — faults, folds, intrusions — plotted onto a map before a single hole gets drilled; the oldest surviving one, the Turin papyrus, mapped Egyptian gold deposits 3,000 years ago.

name: Target Generation
fact: Small basaltic intrusions and dense ore bodies both distort a magnetic field enough to show up as an anomaly — where the anomaly lines up with the mapped geology is where the drill gets pointed.

name: Exploration Drilling
fact: A diamond-set bit wears away as it cuts, exposing fresh diamonds underneath — the same wearing action Rodolphe Leschot's 1863 core bit ran on.

name: Resource Estimation
fact: A deposit gets carved into thousands of identically sized blocks, each one assigned its own grade — that block model is where a mine's tonnage and grade actually come from.

name: Feasibility Study
fact: Scoping, pre-feasibility and definitive feasibility studies get progressively more precise about the same question: will this deposit actually turn a profit.

name: Haul Road
fact: Built to the haul truck fleet's own weight and turning circle, not to any public road standard — width, grade and subbase all sized around the machine, not the other way round.

name: Mine Infrastructure
fact: A power plant, water-management ponds and a camp to house the workforce, all built before a single tonne of ore moves.

name: Overburden
fact: Soil and rock with no value at all, sitting on top of the deposit — has to come off first, every time, before the ore underneath is reachable.

name: Bench
fact: An open pit isn't one hole — it's a stack of stepped terraces, each one worked, drilled and hauled a level at a time.

name: Nitric Acid
fact: Made by burning ammonia over hot platinum — the Ostwald process, still how nearly all of the world's supply gets made.

name: Ammonium Nitrate
fact: Doesn't burn on its own, but as an oxidiser it will accelerate almost anything else that does — which is exactly why it ends up in explosives.

name: ANFO
fact: 94% ammonium nitrate prills soaked in 6% fuel oil — cheap and easy enough to mix at the borehole that it's now the mining industry's default explosive.

name: Blasting
fact: Rows of drilled holes, loaded and detonated in a timed sequence — the step that actually breaks rock too solid for any bucket to just dig into.

name: Excavator
fact: Hydraulic pumps, not cables and gears, drive the bucket — the actual 'load' half of load-and-haul.

name: Run-of-Mine
fact: Raw material exactly as it exists in the mine — loaded and hauled out, but not yet crushed, sorted or processed in any way.

name: Waste Rock
fact: Mined, but never processed — it's fragmented by the same blast as the ore next to it and simply has nowhere useful to go.

name: Waste Dump
fact: Also called a spoil tip, boney pile, or mine dump depending where you are — an engineered pile, not just wherever a truck happens to tip its load.

name: Assay
fact: Accurate to one part in ten thousand on a bead of gold — still the most reliable way there is to measure exactly how much precious metal a rock actually holds.

name: Grade Control
fact: Every load gets checked against the cut-off grade — the minimum worth processing at all — before it's allowed anywhere near the mill.

name: Magnetic Separation
fact: Magnetite needs just one kilogauss of field strength to respond — weak enough that a modest magnet is all it takes to pull it out of a ground-ore stream.

name: Gravity Separation
fact: No chemicals, low cost — density alone does the sorting, the same trick placer mining uses, just built into a machine.

name: Concentrate
fact: What's left once nearly all the worthless rock is gone — a flotation copper concentrate can run 25-30% metal against roughly 0.5% in the ore it came from.

name: Cyanide
fact: One carbon atom triple-bonded to one nitrogen atom, CN⁻ — simple enough that it also turns up naturally in interstellar clouds and comets.

name: Doré Bar
fact: A semi-pure gold-silver alloy, at least 70% precious metal by weight — an unrefined bar poured on-site, not yet investment-grade metal.

name: Heap Leach
fact: Recovers roughly 60-70% of the copper in a heap of crushed low-grade ore — lower than a mill manages, but cheap enough on ore that low-grade to be worth it anyway.

name: Copper Cathode
fact: 99.99% pure — the actual traded commodity form, whether it got there by smelting and electrorefining or by heap leach and electrowinning.

name: Copper Matte
fact: 30 to 70% copper, still mixed with iron sulfide — most of the impurities smelting hasn't burned off yet.

name: Blister Copper
fact: About 98% pure — named for the pitted surface sulfur dioxide gas leaves behind as it escapes while the metal cools.

name: Tailings Dam
fact: Designed, unlike almost anything else a mine builds, to hold its contents forever — often raised in stages using the tailings themselves as fill.

name: Road Freight
fact: Zimbabwe alone trucked roughly 1.13 million tons of spodumene concentrate to port in 2025, before a dedicated rail line existed to replace it.

name: Slurry Pipeline
fact: Tasmania's Savage River pipeline has carried iron concentrate slurry 85km since 1967, on one span 167 metres above the river below it.

name: Car Dumper
fact: A 1909 rotary car dumper could already empty five loaded mine cars a minute; modern ones rotate a car without even uncoupling it from the train.

name: Port Stockpile
fact: Built far bigger than anything the mine itself needed — the whole point is blending trainload after trainload into one grade a ship can load from without stopping.

name: Stacker-Reclaimer
fact: One machine stacks incoming ore into the yard; the other, often the very same gantry, pulls it back off again — blending as it goes.

name: Ship Loader
fact: Its boom moves front to back and up and down on separate drives, so it can reach every part of a hold as the ship's own draught deepens while it fills.

name: Shango
fact: Yoruba orisha of thunder, lightning and drumming; deified after his reign as the third Alaafin of Oyo.

name: Obatala
fact: Yoruba orisha of creation and purity, called King of White Cloth; molded humankind from clay and water.

name: Orisha
fact: The Yoruba pantheon of intermediary spirits sent by Olodumare; tradition numbers them at four hundred and one.

name: Eshu
fact: Yoruba trickster-messenger orisha who carries sacrifices between humans and the other orisha.

name: Elegua
fact: Guardian of roads and crossroads in Cuban Santeria, given the keys to past, present and future by Olodumare.

name: Olorun
fact: Supreme Yoruba sky god, also called Olodumare; worshipped indirectly, through the orisha he sends to earth.

name: Yemoja
fact: Yoruba river goddess, her name means 'mother of fish children'; became a sea goddess in the diaspora.

name: Anansi
fact: Akan trickster spider who won ownership of the sky god Nyame's stories -- still told today as Anansi tales.

name: Oya
fact: Yoruba orisha of storms and the Niger River who can shapeshift into a buffalo; guardian of the ancestral dead.

name: Babalu-Aye
fact: Yoruba orisha of epidemic disease, his body wrapped in palm straw; also known as Sopona or Omolu.

name: Abassi
fact: Efik supreme creator god who forbade the first humans to farm or have children; both rules were broken.

name: Bumba
fact: Kuba (Bushongo) creator god who vomited up the sun, moon, stars and every animal out of primordial darkness.

name: Lotus
fact: Aquatic flower rooted in mud; a 1,300-year-old seed from a dry lakebed still germinated when planted in 1994.

name: Swan
fact: One of the heaviest birds still capable of flight, favoring slow rivers and larger lakes.

name: Veena
fact: A South Asian string instrument, traditionally built from hollowed wood and a gourd resonator.

name: Conch
fact: A large sea snail's shell; with its spire tip cut off, it becomes a blown ceremonial trumpet.

name: Trident
fact: A three-pronged spear, used to harpoon fish and, forged in iron, carried as a weapon.

name: Mouse
fact: A small rodent that thrives in fields and farmland as readily as in houses, alongside people.

name: Monkey
fact: Old and New World monkeys together number well over 200 species, most of them tree-dwelling.

name: Brahma
fact: Four-headed Hindu creator deity, one head reciting each of the four Vedas; his mount is a swan.

name: Vishnu
fact: Hindu preserver god; reclines on the serpent Shesha in the cosmic ocean, holding a conch and lotus.

name: Shiva
fact: Hindu destroyer god; carries a trishula trident, body ash-covered, a cobra coiled at his neck.

name: Saraswati
fact: Hindu goddess of knowledge and the arts; plays the veena, a hamsa (swan) resting at her feet.

name: Lakshmi
fact: Hindu goddess of wealth; four-armed, seated on a lotus, gold coins pouring from one hand.

name: Parvati
fact: Hindu goddess, daughter of the Himalayan king Himavan; mother of Ganesha, her mounts a lion and tiger.

name: Durga
fact: Hindu warrior goddess with up to eighteen arms, each bearing a weapon; slew the buffalo demon Mahishasura.

name: Kali
fact: Fierce Hindu goddess of time and death, garlanded with skulls; calmed by standing on Shiva's chest.

name: Ganesha
fact: Elephant-headed Hindu god of beginnings, one tusk broken; rides a mouse and removes obstacles.

name: Hanuman
fact: Monkey god and son of Vayu; carried an entire Himalayan herb-mountain to Lanka to save Lakshmana.

name: Indra
fact: King of the Hindu devas; wields the thunderbolt vajra and rides the white elephant Airavata.

name: Agni
fact: Hindu fire god and messenger between humans and gods; exists as fire on earth, lightning in the sky.

name: Surya
fact: Hindu sun god, driven across the sky in a chariot pulled by seven horses, Aruna at the reins.

name: Vayu
fact: Hindu wind god and father of Hanuman; revered in the Upanishads as prana, the world's life-breath.

name: Axon
fact: A neuron's single output cable, sometimes over a metre long in a human leg, built to carry one electrical impulse away from the cell.

name: Dendrite
fact: A branching antenna studded with receptor proteins, built to catch neurotransmitter signals arriving from other cells.

name: Neuron
fact: A cell body flanked by branching dendrites and a single long axon — roughly half the brain's 86 billion cells are built this way.

name: Glia
fact: Roughly half the brain's cells, and none of them fire a signal — they feed, insulate, and clean up after the neurons that do.

name: Astrocyte
fact: Star-shaped glial cells that wrap around brain capillaries and decide what crosses from blood into brain tissue.

name: Oligodendrocyte
fact: A glial cell built to manufacture myelin, the fatty membrane that insulates a nearby axon.

name: Myelin Sheath
fact: Concentric wraps of fatty membrane coiled around an axon, letting an impulse jump gap to gap instead of crawling the whole length.

name: Synapse
fact: The junction between two neurons — a gap of about 20 nanometres that only a chemical messenger, not electricity, can cross directly.

name: Neurotransmitter
fact: A chemical messenger, packaged in vesicles and dumped into a synaptic cleft the instant an arriving impulse lets calcium in.

name: Choline
fact: The amine head-group of phosphatidylcholine, the most abundant phospholipid in a cell membrane, and the raw material for one neurotransmitter.

name: Acetylcholine
fact: Choline with an acetyl group stapled on. Released at the neuromuscular junction, it is the one neurotransmitter nerve agents and nicotine both target.

name: Dopamine
fact: Built from tyrosine in two enzyme steps. Reuptake of it is exactly what cocaine blocks, flooding the receiving neuron's receptors.

name: Serotonin
fact: Built from tryptophan in two enzyme steps — the reason tryptophan-rich food gets credited, correctly or not, with lifting mood.

name: Glutamate
fact: The same molecule that builds proteins as glutamic acid does a second job once packaged into a synaptic vesicle: the brain's main excitatory signal.

name: GABA
fact: One enzyme away from glutamate, its own excitatory opposite — snip a carboxyl group off and the brain's chief excitatory signal becomes its chief inhibitory one.

name: Noradrenaline
fact: Dopamine plus one oxygen atom, added by an enzyme that borrows it straight from the air. Drives arousal and the fight-or-flight response.

name: White Matter
fact: Long-range nerve fibers sheathed in fatty myelin — about 60 percent of the brain's tissue by volume, wiring its regions to each other.

name: Gray Matter
fact: Densely packed neuron cell bodies and their synapses, forming the brain's thin, wrinkled outer layer and the cores of its deeper nuclei.

name: Cerebral Cortex
fact: A folded sheet about 2.5 millimetres thick, six layers of gray matter over a bed of white matter, doing sensory processing, language, and conscious experience.

name: Spinal Cord
fact: About 45 centimetres of nerve tracts wrapped around a butterfly-shaped core of gray matter, running from the brain stem down through the vertebral column.

name: Brain Stem
fact: The stalk linking thalamus, forebrain, and spinal cord — its midbrain, pons, and medulla run the reflexes and rhythms that keep a body alive without being asked.

name: Thalamus
fact: A thumb-sized relay station between cortex and lower brain. Every sense but smell is routed through it before the cortex gets to process it.

name: Hypothalamus
fact: A finger-tip-sized cluster of nuclei below the thalamus, running temperature, hunger, thirst, sleep, and the hormone system that keeps the body in balance.

name: Pituitary Gland
fact: A pea-sized gland taking direct orders from the hypothalamus — one lobe is even made of the hypothalamus's own nerve tissue, extended down a stalk.

name: Hippocampus
fact: A seahorse-shaped fold of gray matter where new memories first form, before they're gradually handed off to the cortex for permanent storage.

name: Amygdala
fact: A pair of almond-shaped nuclei tucked in the medial temporal lobe, best known for attaching fear to a stimulus and holding onto it.

name: Corpus Callosum
fact: A dense band of white-matter tracts that is the brain's biggest single connection: everything one hemisphere knows can cross it to reach the other.

name: Cerebrum
fact: The two-hemisphere bulk of the forebrain, cortex on the outside and joined across the middle by the corpus callosum — about 90 percent of the brain's weight.

name: Cerebellum
fact: The 'little brain' behind the brain stem, its own tightly folded gray-matter surface holding more neurons than the rest of the brain put together.

name: Hindbrain
fact: The evolutionarily oldest part of the brain — cerebellum plus brain stem — running the reflexes and movement coordination a body cannot live without.

name: Brain
fact: About 86 billion neurons and roughly as many glia, split into a forebrain that does the thinking and a smaller midbrain and hindbrain that keep the body running.

name: Frontal Lobe
fact: The cortex's front quarter, home to the primary motor cortex that sends the corticospinal tract down to the spinal cord to move the body on command.

name: Parietal Lobe
fact: The cortex region the thalamus routes touch and body-position signals into — where a scattered sense of skin and joints becomes one coherent map of the body.

name: Temporal Lobe
fact: The lobe that houses the amygdala at its medial edge, and on its surface carries the language and emotion processing the amygdala's neighbourhood implies.

name: Occipital Lobe
fact: The cortex's rearmost lobe, reached by the optic radiation — a thick, myelinated white-matter tract that is vision's last stop before it becomes seeing.

name: Meninges
fact: Three membranes — dura, arachnoid, and pia mater — wrapped around the brain so it never has to touch bone directly.

name: Cerebrospinal Fluid
fact: A liter of fluid, mostly water, made inside the brain's own ventricles and replaced three to four times a day, floating the brain so its own weight can't crush it.

name: Blood-Brain Barrier
fact: Tight junctions between capillary cells, policed by astrocyte end-feet, that keep most of what's in the blood from ever reaching brain tissue.

name: Cranial Nerve
fact: One of 12 nerve pairs that connect straight to the brain rather than routing through the spinal cord — 10 of them plug directly into the brain stem.

name: Spinal Nerve
fact: One of 31 nerve pairs, one above each vertebra, each splitting into a sensory branch heading up and a motor branch heading back out to the body.

name: Peripheral Nervous System
fact: Every nerve outside the brain and spinal cord — built from the spinal nerves and cranial nerves that branch out to reach the entire body.

name: Central Nervous System
fact: The brain and spinal cord together — the two organs the rest of the nervous system exists to serve and connect to.

name: Nervous System
fact: Central plus peripheral: an organ system so extensive that all of one body's nerves, laid end to end, could circle the Earth two and a half times.

name: Autonomic Nervous System
fact: The involuntary branch of the peripheral nervous system, run by the hypothalamus, that keeps heart rate, digestion, and breathing going without being asked.

name: Sympathetic Nervous System
fact: The autonomic branch that emerges from the spinal cord's chest and abdominal segments to run the fight-or-flight response.

name: Parasympathetic Nervous System
fact: The autonomic branch carried chiefly by the cranial nerves, running the rest-and-digest state that undoes what sympathetic activation just did.

name: Short-Term Memory
fact: A held pattern of ongoing synaptic activity in the frontal lobe's prefrontal cortex, gone within seconds unless something consolidates it.

name: Long-Term Memory
fact: What a short-term memory becomes once the hippocampus finishes gradually reorganizing it into the cortex's own long-lived networks.

name: Neuroplasticity
fact: Cells that fire together wire together: a synapse used repeatedly recruits more receptors and strengthens, while an unused one fades.

name: Neurogenesis
fact: Neural stem cells dividing into working neurons — in adult mammals this still happens in the hippocampus, though how much it happens in adult humans is genuinely contested.

name: Hippopotamus
fact: Grazes grasslands by night and cools in the river by day; its skin oozes a reddish natural sunscreen.

name: Jackal
fact: Egypt's 'jackal' turned out on closer genetic inspection to be a distinct wolf species.

name: Ibis
fact: A wading marsh bird, mummified by the millions in antiquity, that had vanished from Egypt by the 1850s.

name: Boat
fact: A hollowed or lashed hull, buoyant long before anyone added a sail or an engine.

name: Egyptian Cobra
fact: North Africa's hooding cobra, delivering venom by direct bite rather than a spray.

name: Heart
fact: Cardiac muscle so packed with mitochondria for oxygen that it almost never fatigues.

name: Ra
fact: Egyptian sun god who crossed the sky by day in one barque and the underworld by night in another.

name: Osiris
fact: Egyptian king of the dead, murdered by his brother Set and made whole again by Isis.

name: Isis
fact: Egypt's most powerful goddess -- a healer and magician who revived Osiris and raised Horus in hiding.

name: Horus
fact: Falcon-headed son of Isis and Osiris; lost his eye to Set in battle, and Thoth restored it.

name: Set
fact: Egyptian god of chaos, storms and the desert who murdered his own brother Osiris.

name: Anubis
fact: Jackal-headed god of embalming who weighed the hearts of the dead against Ma'at's feather.

name: Thoth
fact: Ibis-headed god of writing, wisdom and the moon, also shown as a baboon.

name: Bastet
fact: Cat goddess of Bubastis, daughter of Ra, whose annual festival drew crowds by the hundred thousand.

name: Sobek
fact: Crocodile god of the Nile's waters and marshes, merged with Ra as Sobek-Ra.

name: Hathor
fact: Cow goddess of music and love -- the gentle form the rampaging Sekhmet settled back into.

name: Sekhmet
fact: Lioness goddess of war and plague, daughter of Ra, sent to punish a rebellious humanity.

name: Nephthys
fact: Sister of Isis and wife of Set, who helped gather and mourn Osiris's dismembered body.

name: Nut
fact: Sky goddess arched above her husband Geb, mother of Osiris, Isis, Set and Nephthys.

name: Geb
fact: Earth god whose laughter was said to cause earthquakes; husband of the sky goddess Nut.

name: Shu
fact: God of air and light who forced Geb and Nut apart; fog and cloud were called his own bones.

name: Khnum
fact: Ram-headed god who fashioned human bodies and their life force from clay on a potter's wheel.

name: Ptah
fact: Creator god of Memphis, patron of craftsmen, said to have conceived the world in his heart.

name: Amun
fact: 'The Hidden One' -- a minor Theban god who rose to King of the Gods, merged with Ra as Amun-Ra.

name: Ma'at
fact: Goddess of truth and cosmic order; her ostrich feather was weighed against the hearts of the dead.

name: Khonsu
fact: Moon god of Thebes, son of Amun -- 'the Traveller,' credited with instant miraculous healings.

name: Taweret
fact: Hippopotamus goddess who protected women in childbirth and sided with Horus against Set.

name: Serket
fact: Scorpion goddess who guards against venom, carved guarding Tutankhamun's canopic shrine.

name: Wadjet
fact: Cobra goddess of Lower Egypt who became the uraeus, the rearing serpent on the pharaoh's crown.

name: Apep
fact: The 'World-Encircler' -- a giant serpent that attacked Ra's sun barque every night in the underworld.

name: Raven
fact: A kleptoparasite of wolves -- it trails packs to steal from their kills, and has led wolves to prey.

name: Spear
fact: The oldest wooden spears are 300,000 years old; stone, bronze and iron tips came later, bound on.

name: Hammer
fact: Perhaps the oldest tool with definite evidence: unhafted stone hammerstones date to 3.3 million years ago.

name: Rune
fact: Germanic letters cut in straight strokes -- a horizontal line would split the wood grain.

name: Odin
fact: Chief of the AEsir. His ravens report the world to him each day; he traded an eye for wisdom.

name: Thor
fact: Odin's son, god of thunder. Wields the hammer Mjolnir, gripped only with his iron gloves.

name: Loki
fact: Shapeshifting trickster. As a mare he bore Sleipnir; he also fathered the wolf Fenrir and a serpent.

name: Freyja
fact: Vanir goddess of love and war. Rides a cat-drawn chariot and owns the necklace Brisingamen.

name: Frigg
fact: Odin's wife. Orion's Belt was known in Scandinavia as 'Frigg's Distaff,' her spinning tool.

name: Baldr
fact: Odin and Frigg's son. Every object swore never to harm him except the mistletoe that killed him.

name: Heimdall
fact: Watchman of the rainbow bridge Bifrost. His horn Gjallarhorn will sound the start of Ragnarok.

name: Tyr
fact: God of law and single combat. Lost his right hand in the wolf Fenrir's jaws binding it.

name: Njord
fact: Vanir sea god, father of Freyr and Freyja. His mountain marriage to Skadi failed within nights.

name: Skadi
fact: Giantess of winter and skiing. Chose her husband by his feet alone, expecting the god Baldr.

name: Sif
fact: Thor's wife, her golden hair cut off by Loki and replaced with real gold by dwarven smiths.

name: Bragi
fact: God of poetry, said to have runes carved on his own tongue. Greets the slain into Valhalla.

name: Idun
fact: Keeper of the apples that keep the gods young. The giant Thjazi once stole her, eagle-shaped.

name: Hel
fact: Loki's daughter, half flesh and half corpse. Rules the dead who die of sickness or old age.

name: Vidar
fact: Odin's silent, near-mightiest son. His huge shoe is made to kill the wolf Fenrir.

name: Freyr
fact: Vanir god of harvest, rides the golden boar Gullinbursti; traded his sword for a giantess.

name: Mane
fact: Hair, and only males grow one — starting at adolescence as testosterone rises, full size by about age four.

name: Ossicone
fact: A bone core under skin, not a horn or antler — forms before birth, fuses to the skull only at maturity.

name: Tooth
fact: Enamel is the hardest tissue a body makes — 96% mineral, laid down over a bony root.

name: Trunk
fact: Nose and upper lip, fused in early fetal development. No bone at all — just up to 150,000 muscles.

name: Shoulder Hump
fact: Pure muscle, not fat — a power source for digging that no other living bear has.

name: Sagittal Crest
fact: A ridge of bone down the skull's midline, grown to anchor the muscle that powers a bite.

name: Claw
fact: Keratin sheath over the last bone in a toe — the same protein as hair, horn, and hoof.

name: Cecum
fact: A fermentation chamber off the gut — in a koala, about 2 metres long, the largest of any animal its size.

name: Pouch
fact: A fold of skin over the mammary glands, so young barely past embryo stage can still nurse.

name: Red Blood Cell
fact: Round in almost every mammal — oval in exactly one, a shape that keeps blood moving when dehydrated.

name: Hoof
fact: Keratin grown into a hard wall around a single toe bone that carries the animal's whole weight.

name: Knuckle
fact: Where finger bones meet — some apes lock this joint rigid and walk on the back of it.

name: Nuclear Envelope
fact: A double membrane around the genome, its outer layer wired straight into the ER, perforated by thousands of pores.

name: Endoplasmic Reticulum
fact: A network of membrane tubules threading through the cytoplasm, physically continuous with the nucleus.

name: Rough Endoplasmic Reticulum
fact: Ribosomes stud its outer face, giving it a rough look under the microscope and a job making proteins.

name: Smooth Endoplasmic Reticulum
fact: The same tubular network minus the ribosomes — its business is building lipids, not protein.

name: Nucleolus
fact: The largest thing inside the nucleus, and a ribosome factory with no membrane of its own.

name: Golgi Apparatus
fact: Stacked membrane sacs that take in what the rough ER ships out, then modify, sort and repackage it.

name: Lysosome
fact: A membrane bag of over sixty digestive enzymes, budded straight off the Golgi apparatus.

name: Vacuole
fact: Smaller vesicles fuse into one big one; in a mature plant cell it can fill most of the space.

name: Cytoskeleton
fact: Microtubules plus actin filaments plus intermediate filaments: the scaffolding every cell builds itself from.

name: Centriole
fact: Nine microtubule triplets ringed into a cylinder, always kept in a pair near the nucleus.

name: Cilia
fact: Hundreds of short hairs beating in unison, each built on a nine-plus-two ring of microtubules.

name: Flagella
fact: The same nine-plus-two core as a cilium, just one or two per cell instead of hundreds, and far longer.

name: Cell Wall
fact: A rigid cellulose layer laid down just outside the membrane — a plant cell building its own exoskeleton.

name: Plasmid
fact: A loop of DNA a bacterium keeps on the side, copying itself independently of the main chromosome.

name: Diffusion
fact: Molecules drift from where they're crowded to where they're not — no energy required, no pump needed.

name: Osmosis
fact: Diffusion's special case: water alone, crossing a selective membrane toward wherever solutes are thicker.

name: Active Transport
fact: Moving a substance the wrong way down its own gradient — and it always costs a burnt ATP.

name: Endocytosis
fact: The membrane folds around something outside, pinches shut, and the outside becomes an inside.

name: Exocytosis
fact: The Golgi apparatus's shipping side in action: a vesicle docks at the membrane and empties itself outward.

name: Phagocytosis
fact: A cell doesn't just absorb a bacterium — it wraps its whole membrane around it and swallows it whole.

name: Muscle Cell
fact: Actin ordered into thousands of repeating sarcomeres, burning ATP directly to slide past itself.

name: White Blood Cell
fact: Its lysosomes are loaded and waiting for whatever it engulfs by phagocytosis.

name: Guard Cell
fact: One of the only epidermal cells that keeps its chloroplasts — the other reason it can pump salt and swell.

name: Palisade Cell
fact: Long, tightly packed cylinders under a leaf's upper skin, carrying more chloroplasts than any other leaf cell.

name: Goblet Cell
fact: A secretory cell built around an oversized Golgi apparatus, its whole shape swollen with mucin granules.

name: Mucus
fact: Ninety to ninety-five percent water; the rest is mucin, and together they trap whatever the air brings in.

name: Ciliated Cell
fact: Hundreds of beating hairs on one cell, sweeping the trachea's mucus blanket up and out.

name: Blood
fact: Mostly plasma by volume, but the two kinds of cell suspended in it do entirely different jobs.

name: Nitrogen Gas
fact: N2 — two nitrogen atoms locked by a triple bond so strong almost nothing can break it, which is why it makes up 78% of the air and does almost nothing while it is there.

name: Fox
fact: Most widely distributed member of the dog family, found across the entire Northern Hemisphere.

name: Bow
fact: A flexed stave that stores energy in its limbs, released through a string to launch an arrow.

name: Taiko
fact: Japanese drum family with cowhide heads stretched over a wooden shell, beaten with sticks.

name: Izanagi
fact: Primordial Shinto god who churned the sea into Japan's islands, then fled the underworld Yomi in horror.

name: Izanami
fact: Primordial Shinto goddess who died bearing the fire god Kagutsuchi and became ruler of the underworld Yomi.

name: Amaterasu
fact: Shinto sun goddess and mythical ancestor of Japan's imperial line; hid in a cave, darkening the world.

name: Susanoo
fact: Shinto storm god exiled from Heaven for his rampage; slew the eight-headed serpent Yamata-no-Orochi.

name: Tsukuyomi
fact: Shinto moon god who killed the food goddess Uke Mochi in disgust, forever separating day from night.

name: Kagutsuchi
fact: Shinto fire god; his birth killed his mother Izanami, so his father beheaded and dismembered him in revenge.

name: Inari
fact: Shinto kami of rice, fertility and industry, whose messengers are white foxes -- kitsune.

name: Ryujin
fact: Shinto dragon king of the sea, ruling a palace of red and white coral beneath the waves.

name: Fujin
fact: Shinto wind god, one of the eldest kami, shown carrying a huge bag of winds on his shoulders.

name: Raijin
fact: Shinto thunder god who beats drums ringed with the tomoe symbol from atop the clouds.

name: Hachiman
fact: Shinto god of war and archery, syncretic spirit of Emperor Ojin; guardian kami of the samurai.

name: Tenjin
fact: Shinto god of scholarship -- the deified spirit of the exiled courtier-poet Sugawara no Michizane.

name: Uke Mochi
