fact: Shinto food goddess killed by Tsukuyomi; crops and livestock grew from her corpse afterward.

name: Mikaboshi
fact: Shinto star god, the only deity who refused to submit to the heavenly gods' conquest of the earth.

name: Ame-no-Iwato
fact: The heavenly rock cave where Amaterasu hid after Susanoo's rampage, plunging the world into darkness.

name: Ame-no-Uzume
fact: Shinto goddess of dawn and mirth; her bawdy dance lured Amaterasu out of hiding and founded kagura dance.

name: Sarutahiko
fact: Shinto guardian kami with a seven-span nose and eyes like mirrors; blocked the descent of the heavenly gods.

name: Tectonic Plate
fact: Earth's brittle outer shell broken into semirigid slabs — seven major ones, a dozen or so smaller.

name: Divergent Boundary
fact: Where two plates pull apart and magma rises to freeze into new crust, mostly along mid-ocean ridges.

name: Convergent Boundary
fact: Where two plates are driven together — one dives beneath the other, or both crumple upward instead.

name: Transform Boundary
fact: Where two plates grind sideways past one another along a fault, neither building crust nor destroying it.

name: Earthquake
fact: The ground's sudden release of strain built up along a locked fault, radiating out as seismic waves.

name: Mid-Ocean Ridge
fact: A continuous seam of brand-new seafloor, welling up along a divergent boundary for about 65,000 km.

name: Taxonomy
fact: The nested system — kingdom down to species — that gives every living thing exactly one place and one name.

name: Tree of Life
fact: A branching diagram connecting every classified group of life back through common ancestry.

name: Cladistics
fact: Grouping organisms by shared derived traits, not overall looks — the method behind the whale-hippo surprise.

name: Island
fact: Land walled in by water on every side. Isolation is exactly what makes island wildlife so distinctive.

name: Fossil
fact: Ancient remains preserved in rock after minerals slowly replace the original bone or shell.

name: Genetic Drift
fact: Random, chance shifts in a population's allele frequencies — strongest of all in small populations.

name: Gene Flow
fact: Alleles moving between populations as individuals, pollen, or seeds cross from one to another.

name: Adaptation
fact: A trait shaped over generations by natural selection to fit its bearer to its environment.

name: Sexual Selection
fact: Mate choice or rivalry favouring traits that win breeding success, not just plain survival.

name: Artificial Selection
fact: Humans, not nature, choosing which individuals breed — the same mechanism, a different judge.

name: Reproductive Isolation
fact: Populations diverged enough that they can no longer produce fertile offspring together.

name: Speciation
fact: The point at which diverging populations can no longer interbreed and become separate species.

name: Adaptive Radiation
fact: One ancestral population fanning rapidly into many species, each fit to a different niche.

name: Homology
fact: Shared underlying structure — the same bone plan in a wing, a flipper, and a hand — from common descent.

name: Vestigial Structure
fact: A once-useful body part reduced to a nonfunctional leftover once selection stopped favouring it.

name: Fossil Record
fact: The total, ordered archive of fossils across rock strata — evolution's clearest paper trail.

name: Transitional Fossil
fact: A fossil bridging two groups, carrying features of both the ancestral and the descendant form.

name: Living Fossil
fact: A living species so little changed from its fossil relatives it looks like it stepped out of deep time.

name: Extinction
fact: The permanent disappearance of a species when the last individual dies without descendants.

name: Mass Extinction
fact: A sudden, global loss of a large share of species all at once, resetting evolution's course.

name: Camouflage
fact: Colouring or pattern that blends its bearer into the background — adaptation you can see at a glance.

name: Peacock
fact: A pheasant relative native to South Asia; males spread an iridescent, eye-marked tail in courtship.

name: Owl
fact: Comb-like serrations on its flight feathers muffle the wingbeat, letting it hunt almost silently.

name: Helmet
fact: Protective head covering; Bronze Age Aegean warriors wore bronze and boar's-tusk designs.

name: Lyre
fact: Ancient stringed instrument; its classic form used a hollowed tortoise shell as a soundbox.

name: Poppy
fact: The scarlet corn poppy grows wild among cereal crops; a different species yields opium.

name: Arrow
fact: A projectile shaft tipped with a point -- among the oldest weapons humans have made.

name: Cicada
fact: Nymphs feed on root sap underground for years before emerging to moult into winged adults.

name: Cerberus
fact: Three-headed dog, offspring of Echidna and Typhon, that guards the gates of the underworld.

name: Zeus
fact: King of the Olympian gods, ruler of sky and thunder. Roman Jupiter. Won his throne from the Titans.

name: Hera
fact: Queen of the gods and goddess of marriage. Roman Juno. Homeric epithet Boopis, 'cow-eyed.'

name: Poseidon
fact: God of the sea and earthquakes, 'the Earth-Shaker.' Roman Neptune. Carries a trident.

name: Hades
fact: God of the dead and ruler of the underworld. Roman Pluto. Also called Plouton, 'the rich one.'

name: Athena
fact: Goddess of wisdom and war strategy. Roman Minerva. Sprang fully armed from Zeus's head.

name: Apollo
fact: God of prophecy, music and archery. Chief epithet Phoebus, 'bright.' Twin brother of Artemis.

name: Artemis
fact: Goddess of the hunt, wilderness and the moon. Roman Diana. Twin sister of Apollo.

name: Ares
fact: God of war and battle-frenzy. Roman Mars. Called by Zeus 'the most hateful of all gods.'

name: Aphrodite
fact: Goddess of love and beauty. Roman Venus. Name means 'foam-arisen,' born of the sea.

name: Hermes
fact: Messenger of the gods and guide of souls to the underworld. Roman Mercury. Patron of travelers and thieves.

name: Dionysus
fact: God of wine, ecstasy and theatre. Roman Bacchus. Called the 'twice-born' god.

name: Demeter
fact: Goddess of grain and the harvest. Roman Ceres. Her grief for Persephone brings winter.

name: Persephone
fact: Queen of the underworld and goddess of spring growth. Roman Proserpina. Daughter of Demeter.

name: Hephaestus
fact: God of fire, the forge and craftsmen. Roman Vulcan. Epithet Amphigyeeis, 'the lame one.'

name: Cronus
fact: Titan king who ruled the Golden Age. Roman Saturn. Overthrew his father Uranus, and was overthrown by Zeus.

name: Gaia
fact: Primordial personification of the Earth. Roman Terra. Mother of Uranus and the Titans.

name: Uranus
fact: Primordial personification of the sky, first ruler of the cosmos. Castrated by his son Cronus.

name: Rhea
fact: Titaness of motherhood, wife of Cronus. Roman Ops. Saved infant Zeus with a trick of stone and cloth.

name: Eros
fact: God of desire and love. Roman Cupid. Ovid gives him gold arrows that kindle love and lead ones that repel it.

name: Nike
fact: Winged personification of victory. Roman Victoria. Daughter of the Titan Pallas and the river Styx.

name: Helios
fact: God who personifies the sun. Roman Sol. Drives a four-horse chariot across the sky each day.

name: Selene
fact: Goddess who personifies the moon. Roman Luna. Sister of Helios and Eos.

name: Eos
fact: Goddess who personifies the dawn. Roman Aurora. Homer's constant epithet: 'rosy-fingered.'

name: Pan
fact: God of the wild, shepherds and flocks. Roman Faunus. Has the legs and horns of a goat.

name: Hypnos
fact: God who personifies sleep. Roman Somnus. Twin brother of Thanatos, death, and son of Nyx, night.

name: Heracles
fact: Greatest of the Greek heroes. Roman Hercules. Son of Zeus, famed for his Twelve Labors.

name: Odysseus
fact: King of Ithaca, hero of the Odyssey. Roman Ulysses. Known for his cunning, metis.

name: Indian Rhinoceros
fact: Wart-like bumps armor its deeply folded skin — adults face almost no natural predator.

name: Spotted Hyena
fact: A bite 40% stronger than a leopard's lets it crush bone that would defeat most carnivores.

name: Sloth
fact: Leaves can take more than a month to digest — no other mammal's gut works that slowly.

name: Three-Banded Armadillo
fact: The only armadillo that can roll its whole body into a sealed, armored ball.

name: Hedgehog
fact: Its spines are just hair, stiffened with keratin — and two back muscles roll it into a spiky, sealed ball.

name: Meerkat
fact: Eye sockets covering over a fifth of its skull power the binocular vision behind its sentry watch.

name: Large Intestine
fact: Cecum, colon, rectum, anal canal in series — built to reclaim water and salt, not absorb nutrients.

name: Colon
fact: Ascending, transverse, descending, sigmoid — one tube bent twice, by the liver then the spleen.

name: Haustra
fact: Segmented pouches once blamed on short muscle bands — now thought to be the enteric nervous system's work.

name: Rectum
fact: Where the colon's muscle bands blend into one sheath and the pouches vanish: a smooth reservoir for feces.

name: Appendix
fact: Reassessed since the early 2000s: not vestigial. Its wall is packed with immune tissue standing watch.

name: Peristalsis
fact: A wave of muscle: relax ahead, contract behind. The colon mostly skips it for a few big daily pushes.

name: Gut Flora
fact: The body's largest bacterial ecosystem — a relationship that's mutualistic, not just commensal.

name: Vitamin K
fact: Gut bacteria — E. coli among them — convert it between forms and can synthesize their own share.
